Headline: I was born in Kentucky at a time when my parents’ marriage was illegal.A high school guidance counselor told me I shouldn’t go to college — because I’m half Black, and “Black people don’t do well in college.”I went anyway.5 degrees later — including my PhD — I’ve spent nearly two decades doing work that wasn’t supposed to be mine to do.I co-founded the first NP-owned practice in Louisville. I became the first PhD-prepared nurse hired as an attending at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, a role that had only ever gone to physicians. I’ve led multi-million-dollar research initiatives in cancer prevention and behavioral science, built community health programs that reach thousands, and helped change how we talk about lung cancer screening, stigma, and health equity at a national level.And I’ve done it all while living between two cities — honoring both my marriage and my calling, even when people said it couldn’t work.Here’s what all of that taught me:The lanes we’re told to stay in aren’t real. The barriers we’re told we can’t cross are often just doors no one’s opened yet. And the most powerful leadership doesn’t come from titles or credentials — it comes from returning to who you actually are.That’s the work I do now.I work in two lanes. Soul to Soul Leadership is my weekly newsletter and podcast for leaders who climbed the ladder and lost the thread. I write about what high-achievement costs us — and how we find our way back. Join me at https://soultosoulleadership.substack.com/ Lost In Translation is the NIH grantsmanship curriculum I built after years of watching brilliant science fail in review — not because the ideas were weak, but because something got lost between the researcher's mind and the reviewer's page. It's a 14-module system built around Five Translation Gaps, aligned with the NIH 2025 Simplified Review Framework, and currently in use at Mayo Clinic, Georgetown Lombardi, and Hackensack Meridian Health. → Start free: www.lisacarterbawa.com/module1 → Full curriculum: www.lisacarterbawa.com/losttranslation → Institutional programs, R01 reviews, and speaking: email me at lisa@soultosoulleadership.com  The professional version:Founding Director, CPPCI, Center for Discovery & Innovation, Hackensack Meridian Health Deputy Associate Director, Community Outreach & Engagement, Georgetown Lombardi Professor of Oncology, Georgetown University Professor of Medicine, Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine NIH-funded behavioral scientist | $22M+ in research funding PhD | MPH | APRN | ANP-C | FAAN | FSBM

Headline: After nearly 30 years of experience helping others face cancer, I consider “difficult conversations” a core sub-specialty of my oncology and hematology practice.   My Backstory My dad was diagnosed with leukemia when I was in high school. Understanding his disease was a struggle for my family. It took time and numerous conversations with doctors, but the more my dad understood his options, the more he began to make choices that allowed him to face cancer his way. His approach to cancer became one of the most important lesson on living that I ever received.  When I became an oncologist, I didn’t just want to treat the disease; I wanted to treat the entire experience of life with cancer. So, I came up with simple analogies and stories based on my personal experiences to help patients and families make sense of what was happening. My hope was to empower them to live despite cancer, as my dad had done.   These conversations eventually inspired a book, How Cancer Is Like a Dandelion, but it wasn’t until my daughter, Abby, developed a rare medical condition that I fully understood how transformative conversations can be. Turning confusing information into simple, human conversation became a lifeline for Abby, allowing her to move past the fear and anxiety she felt and on to living her life.   After Abby’s experience, we both developed a new calling in life—to share the unique, patient-centered language we created with other professionals in the medical community who face difficult conversations every day.   What is Leveling Health Publishing? Leveling Health is a health information resource that providers and organizations in healthcare, pharmaceuticals, health tech, and health education can share with patients and partners to provide clear, straightforward, compassionate answers to complex or sensitive medical questions. Backed by a team of medical and educational experts, our customizable, easy-to-understand health content helps prepare patients for important conversations, and deepens their bond with healthcare professionals to create a more meaningful patient experience.  Building confidence. Improving outcomes. Leveling Health.
